new_statements.reading: Primary stress is word-initial by default (first syllable of the first stress group); a lexically restricted stress-shift rule moves primary (and secondary) stress one syllable rightward onto /a/ when the initial syllable has a high vowel and no intervening voiceless stop (about 2% of words, plus six unexplained residue words), and durative reduplication also yields non-initial primary stress. Secondary stresses fall on the first syllable of each following stress group (1-3 syllables, cluster-bounded). This is the catalog's own deciding source read first-hand; it confirms 'fixed initial' with a small /a/-attraction exception class. Two refinements: the 'normally have primary stress on the first syllable' sentence is on printed p.18 (not p.17), and the §5.5 two-percent second-syllable class should be noted. Waters 1989 (PL C-114, p.xv) agrees: 'non-contrastive vowel length may occur in the primary-stressed syllable, which is usually the first syllable of a word.'

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (primary stress word-initial): 'Ordinarily, primary stress falls on the initial syllable of a word.' It refines Waters 1980b by recasting the cluster-bounded stress groups as quantity-sensitive secondary stress on heavy CVC syllables (plus [+distributed]-onset syllables), by treating the /a/-driven second-syllable class as a metrical Move-x rule bounded to one syllable rightward with /a/ underlyingly geminate, and by giving a lexical-cyclic metrical (tree+grid) analysis. The stress-shift facts (one syllable rightward, /a/ attraction, durative reduplication) match Waters 1980b §5.5 and §7, on whose data (Waters 1980a, 1980b) the paper is explicitly built. Not a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress ordinarily falls on the first syllable of the word. Secondary stress is quantity-sensitive: it falls on heavy (CVC) syllables and on the initial syllable of each subsequent stress group, and syllables beginning with a [+distributed] (laminal) consonant also tend to begin a stress group and take secondary stress. A stress-shift rule (Move x on a mixed tree-plus-grid representation) can move primary stress at most one syllable rightward, driven by /a/ (which Obrst treats as underlyingly geminate, i.e. a complex rime attracting stress) and by durative reduplication of the root-initial syllable; the shift is to increase eurhythmy, not to avoid clash. Stress assignment is lexical/cyclic ('applying twice: first at the root..').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated explicitly: on heavy (CVC) syllables 'observing quantity sensitivity' and on the initial syllable of each stress group; syllables with [+distributed] consonant onsets frequently begin a stress group and receive secondary stress. Obrst compares the system to Prince's Koya type (first syllable plus all heavy syllables stressed).
new_statements.exceptions: Primary stress shifts one syllable rightward (initial to second syllable) when /a/ attracts it (analysed as a geminate / complex rime) and under durative reduplication; some shift cases in ex. (23) are 'not due to the presence of /a/'. Obrst also cites Waters's statement that no function word, pronoun, or.. (snippet cut) takes part in the pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: Obrst's data are Waters's Djinang (Waters 1980a, 1980b); no dialect or clan variety is named in the snippets. The scanned/snippet text spells the language 'Djinan' (title 'Stress and Stress-Related Phenomena in Djinan') — this is the same language, glottocode djin1253, not a different variety. The Glottolog/OZBIB citation ('Transactions of the Royal Literary Fund 31', 1989) is a corrupted entry for this same paper.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the word-initial syllable by default; secondary stress on heavy (CVC) syllables and on stress-group-initial syllables (often those with [+distributed] onsets); a metrical Move-x rule shifts stress at most one syllable rightward (the /a/-attraction and durative-reduplication cases), in a tree+grid lexical-cyclic analysis built on Waters 1980a/b data.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Quantity-sensitive: heavy (CVC) syllables and stress-group-initial syllables (incl. [+distributed]-onset syllables) receive secondary stress (snippets 114, 201, 206).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift one syllable rightward (Move x), attributed to /a/ (argued underlyingly geminate) and to durative reduplication of the root-initial syllable; a residue of shift cases 'not due to the presence of /a/' (snippets 103-104, 211-212).
new_statements.identity_note: Djinang (Obrst's scanned running text spells it 'Djinan'), Yolngu (Murngic) group, north-central Arnhem Land; Obrst works from Waters 1980a/1980b data, i.e. the same pooled clan-dialect base as the catalog source.
